Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-15
Time: 16:00 PT
Duration: 58 minutes
Attendees: Ava Chen (Redwood AE), Ravi Patel (Redwood SE), Sofia Ruiz (Redwood Solutions), Maya Lopez (CTO, HelioTech), Jon Park (Sr ML Eng), Liam O'Connor (Infra), Priya Singh (Security)

--- Auto-generated sections (may be imperfect) ---
Summary: triage of KV cache priming causing nondeterministic cudagraph replay and kernel route divergence between TensorRT-LLM and vLLM execution paths.
Topics: KV priming, eviction, cudagraph replay, quantization path locks, VPC on-prem telemetry
Action items: see below

--- Transcript ---
[00:00] Ava Chen: hey everyone thanks for joining, we have about an hour, um goal is to go deep on the KV priming issue you sent and figure out a reproducible sweep and next steps.
[00:18] Maya Lopez: yeah thanks ava, appreciate it. jon and liam will jump in technical. this is affecting our on-prem g4 cluster during p95 workloads, we see latency spikes and occasional cudagraph replay misses.
[00:30] Ravi Patel: cool, quick intro from my side, ravi, runtime perf at Redwood. i looked at the traces you attached; initial thing that sticks out is asymmetric priming — some prefixes populate KV differently which causes a different kernel path to be selected during the replay.
[00:45] Jon Park: when you say kernel path you mean tensorrt-llm vs vllm execution kernels? sometimes we see a switch mid-epoch and the perf drops 2-3x.
[00:58] Ravi Patel: yeah exactly, we saw in similar cases that the exec path tiebreaker picks a TRT-optimized kernel for certain sequence length patterns and a vllm dynamic exec path for others, which then changes how cuda-graph replay is constructed. the cudagraph recorded with one path won't replay cleanly when the kvcache state forces a different path.
[01:22] Sofia Ruiz: note, sometimes cudagraph replay aborts and falls back to eager mode which increases latency but still completes. that fallback is expected, but the nondeterminism and 3x variance is what you're seeing.
[01:36] Liam O'Connor: our cluster is a mixed NVLink rig with heterogeneous memory banks. could that make the graph replay more fragile? we also are running int8 quant on some models.
[01:50] Ravi Patel: yep heterogeneous HW + int8 quantization + asymmetric prefix priming is a cocktail. int8 introduces more kernel variants and small numeric differences that influence kernel selection heuristics. mixed nvlink can affect memory placement and what kernels are available.
[02:05] Jon Park: the times we observe it: after a long tail of streaming requests, the p95 jumps. priming seems correlated: when a long prompt with many prefixes primes the kvcache, subsequent short prompts hit a different path causing replay mismatch.
[02:22] Ava Chen: can you describe your dev repro? you had a small script in the ticket?
[02:30] Jon Park: yes, python client that primes ~2000 tokens across sessions, then issues random short conversational queries. happens ~10% of runs on our dev node. we attached cuda-memcheck and nvprof but the traces are big.
[02:45] Ravi Patel: perfect, that's reproducible enough to triage. first ask — can you capture a pair of traces: one where cudagraph recorded path A and replayed (ok), and one where record is A but replay selects path B (fail)? the nvtx ranges + network_id in the logs help us align.
[03:02] Jon Park: we can, though shipping raw nvprof is heavy — we'll upload to a signed GCS link.
[03:09] Priya Singh: from security side, we need a checklist for what can be shared — redwood in our VPC will need ephemeral creds and we can't share raw prod traces.
[03:20] Ava Chen: understood — we can take dev-only traces and our engineers will operate under your temporary bucket. I'll send the security pack and the minimum trace requirements.
[03:30] Ravi Patel: back to root cause hypotheses: 1) asymmetric KV priming changes the block-sparsity / sequence-length distribution used during cudagraph record which flips a kernel selector heuristic, 2) quantized kernels have different fallback paths when certain occupancy thresholds are hit, 3) cudagraph replay is sensitive to small differences in scratch memory layout — with mixed mem banks that can push the runtime to choose alternate kernels.
[03:55] Maya Lopez: is this more a runtime bug (we expect stable replay) or just an artifact of optimized kernel selection being heuristic?
[04:05] Ravi Patel: it's a bit of both. cudagraph replay is deterministic for identical operator graphs and memory layouts. here the operator graph can diverge because of different kernel variants being chosen at record time vs replay time — the runtime's heuristic is trying to optimize for occupancy and instruction-level throughput. when inputs (KV cache shape, prefetched embeddings) differ, it might choose a different kernel. we have mitigations: lock the execution path (force TRT path), force a deterministic cudagraph record/replay with stricter checks, or make priming more uniform.
[04:39] Jon Park: forcing TRT path sounds attractive, but we worry about quality/regression differences vs vLLM dynamic path. any guidance on tradeoffs?
[04:50] Ravi Patel: tradeoffs: TRT often gives better throughput and lower latency for long sequences but can be brittle across quantization. vLLM dynamic exec is more robust for short bursty requests and prefix variability. if your workload is mixed we recommend canarying a constrained TRT variant and collecting MRR/quality metrics.
[05:10] Sofia Ruiz: additional knob: the cudagraph replay options — there's a 'strict replay' flag that ensures operator layout sanity checks at the cost of record overhead. For queued production traffic we usually enable a relaxed mode for throughput but strict mode for debugging.
[05:28] Liam O'Connor: how invasive is enabling strict replay? can it add 10-20% overhead?
[05:34] Ravi Patel: in our tests strict replay adds 5-12% recording overhead; replay itself stays fast but you might see more fallbacks during record phase. also, it surfaces mismatches early.
[05:47] Jon Park: ok, so next step is run a priming sweep. what parameters should we try?
[05:53] Ravi Patel: start with three priming profiles: symmetric small (uniform 200 token prefixes across sessions), asymmetric low (1k tokens concentrated in 10% of sessions), and asymmetric high (5k concentrated). For each run, capture nvtx/timeline, kernel selection logs (we'll provide a small tracer), and model outputs for quality checks.
[06:12] Maya Lopez: run that on our dev node with int8 and fp16 to compare?
[06:17] Ravi Patel: yes run both quant levels. int8 tends to increase kernel switches. also capture cudagraph create/replay timestamps to measure % replay failures.
[06:26] [short crosstalk]
[06:30] Priya Singh: on the security note, we need to confirm that redwood SE won't request keys or sensitive data. only need perf traces + non-prod data.
[06:38] Ava Chen: we'll confirm scope in writing and send the security checklist.
[06:42] Jon Park: about on-prem constraints — we keep our control plane internal. can redwood tools run inside our VPC?
[06:49] Ava Chen: yes we have Redwood Private options and limited SE-run debugging that can be deployed into a customer's VPC or we can run with envoy-sidecar to capture traces. for now dev node access with an ephemeral key is easiest.
[07:00] Liam O'Connor: would enabling a dedicated GPU pool (like Redwood Dedicated) change anything here? we have capacity but licensing compexity.
[07:08] Ravi Patel: Redwood Dedicated gives predictable kernels because the runtime profile is pinned per pool; that can reduce nondeterminism, but doesn't eliminate priming-induced layout differences entirely. Dedicated helps with throttling and consistent compilers/kernels across nodes.
[07:23] Maya Lopez: are there specific runtime flags you recommend toggling to make cudagraph replay deterministic for the experiment?
[07:30] Ravi Patel: yes — we'll share a small script: set REPLAY_STRICT=1, FORCE_EXEC_PATH=trt (optional), ENABLE_KV_PRIMER_LOG=1. Also an env to disable dynamic kernel fusion temporarily. We'll provide exact flags in the runbook.
[07:47] Jon Park: you mentioned kernel fusion — could that be the point where record vs replay diverge?
[07:53] Ravi Patel: fusion and autotuner caches can cause graph shapes to change slightly; if fusion yields a different operator ordering, the graph recorded won't match replay. Fusion is beneficial but for triage we recommend disabling it to test baseline.
[08:05] Maya Lopez: ok that's clear. what about quantization — you said int8 creates more variants. would switching to fp16 across the cluster be a reasonable mitigation?
[08:14] Ravi Patel: switching to fp16 reduces kernel variant proliferation but increases memory use. It's a trade: fp16 tends to be more stable for cudagraph replay, int8 is higher variance but lower memory/cost. For testing, run both and compare.
[08:26] Sofia Ruiz: also capture a baseline with a tiny warmup — small priming — because sometimes the variance only shows up after long-run priming. document the exact seed and order of prompts.
[08:37] Jon Park: good point, our current script randomizes session order which might hide determinism. we'll lock seed.
[08:42] [pause]
[08:45] Ravi Patel: another angle: the runtime's kernel selection is influenced by occupancy heuristics — we can log the chosen kernel meta and hash alongside NVTX. that will make it trivial to diff record vs replay paths. We have a lightweight tracer that instruments kernel selection. I'll attach it.
[09:02] Ava Chen: we'll also provide the perf-runbook with exact CLI commands and the tracer.
[09:08] Jon Park: any chance this is an nvdriver bug? we've seen driver-level nondeterminism in older stacks.
[09:16] Ravi Patel: possible but less likely. driver bugs usually manifest as correctness issues not just path divergence. still, collect the driver version and CUDA runtime/driver info as part of traces.
[09:27] Liam O'Connor: our infra notes: nvidia driver 525.x, cuda 12.1, mixed gridded nvlink nodes. we'll include exact spec.
[09:35] Priya Singh: we need to know how long redwood will keep traces if we share them. retention policy?
[09:42] Ava Chen: standard is 30 days for SE-received dev traces unless otherwise agreed. we can sign an NDA addendum for longer retention.
[09:50] [crowd murmur]
[09:52] Ravi Patel: ok, hypothesize workflow for triage: 1) capture failing and passing traces, 2) run priming sweep across quant modes and priming profiles, 3) enable strict replay and force exec path variant to isolate variance, 4) compare kernel selection logs and nvtx timeline to find the exact operator that diverges.
[10:12] Jon Park: sounds good. if we find a single operator that flips variant, would a runtime patch to prefer the stable kernel be safe?
[10:20] Ravi Patel: in many cases yes — we can add a fallback to prefer the kernel that matches previous recording under similar env. But doing that broadly might regress perf for other workloads. So we'd propose a per-model/per-route flag or an auto-canary that toggles kernel preference when mismatch rate > threshold.
[10:38] Maya Lopez: what's the expected timeline to get an initial analysis after traces?
[10:42] Ravi Patel: once we have paired traces and priming runs, initial analysis within 3 business days — more if we need to iterate.
[10:49] Ava Chen: schedule check-in for 2026-03-24, send invites.
[10:54] Sofia Ruiz: one more thought: if the cudagraph replay mismatch is caused by small address-space layout differences (heap vs pooled allocator), forcing a pooled allocator for the model can reduce address variance; capture allocator config.
[11:07] Jon Park: we'll add that config to the trace.
[11:11] Priya Singh: please include the list of env vars you need and exact file paths for logs; we need to review before granting access.
[11:18] Ava Chen: will send checklist with exact env vars and minimal logs.
[11:22] Liam O'Connor: if we want redwood to run experiments inside our VPC, what's the onboarding time?
[11:29] Ava Chen: we can stand up a limited SE-run in 48-72 hours once network rules and ephemeral creds are in place. full private deployment is longer but not necessary for triage.
[11:39] Jon Park: ok let's recap the concrete next steps.
[11:42] Ava Chen: recap: 1) Jon/Liam provide failing+passing traces + environment metadata by 2026-03-18; 2) Ravi runs priming sweep on Helio dev cluster (or provide script for them to run) capturing kernel-selection logs and nvtx by 2026-03-22; 3) Ava sends security pack and runbook by 2026-03-17; 4) follow-up triage 2026-03-24.
[12:04] Maya Lopez: that timeline works. thanks all.
[12:08] [03:00 of silence as final logistics are hashed out and links shared]

[15:16] Jon Park: thanks, appreciate it.
